newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK air cargo rates steady to firm on high vol.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK air cargo rates steady to firm on high vol.

text.p: Air cargo volumes ex-UK remained at high year-end levels as Far East demand continues to lead the way, with many average air cargo market rates steady to firmer, a Reuter survey shows.

The almost daily announcement of cargo fuel surcharges by large and smaller carriers, is a key issue amongst airlines, forwarders and shippers. Some 44 ex-London surcharges have been formally notified in writing, one industry source said.
The surcharges are tending to be set at US1O cents a kg, or the equivalent in local currency to all destinations, but some airlines are applying lower charges to short-haul or domestic operations.

A popular date for the introduction of surcharges has been November 15 or just as the special International Air Transport Association (IATA) meeting being held this week in Geneva to consider the issue of higher fuel costs is due to come to an end.

Both forwarders and shippers are unhappy at what they consider to be the short notice involved in many of the surcharges, even if they recognise that jet fuel prices have risen substantially since mid-summer.

British Airways Plc applied a six pence per kg surcharge from November 8 for intercontinental routes and three pence on European and domestic routes. Most other airlines have followed BA, although some have delayed its application.
These include Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd with a start date of November 25 -- and a five pence kg surcharge -- while SAS is waiting until December 1.

Average market rates per kg for 100 kg, and excluding surcharges, to the Far East, are as follows. Tokyo around 2.04 stg, marginally easier than the previous 2.06 with around 1.80 stg on some indirect routes.
Seoul has also firmed up to 1.99 stg a kg per 100 kg from 1.97 kg with Hong Kong and Singapore little changed around the 1.21 stg and 1.28 stg a kg level respectively, the sources said.
Sydney moved to 2.15 stg a kg average per 100 kg from the previous 2.12 stg, they added.

"Business is looking good through to the New Year and as are forecasts for January. Flights are still going out full", said Tony Edwards from Japan Airlines Cargo adding that the carrier expects to take a decision on the cargo fuel surcharge issue on November 19.

"The market is still very good. We've seen record tonnage and revenues in October. Shipments include computer parts and electronic equipment, as well as consumer items such as 30,000 CDs by the British pop group, Spice Girls," All Nippon Airlines' John O'Shea said.
Malaysian Airlines also reported a strong volume and revenue performance in recent weeks with the situation better than at the same time last year, a cargo official said.

"Business is booming with enquiries from many agents. Computer parts are being shipped from Ireland to Penang for added value work and then re-exported.There's also good demand for general cargo," the official added.
"It is also looking good for cargo to both Australia and Korea," he added.
Demand is "excellent and booming to all our Far Eastern markets," said a Cathay Pacific cargo sales official. "The biggest problem is finding capacity on flights," he added.
"We're going out quite full and even carrying some Beaujolais Nouveau to cope with the rise in Asian demand," said Frank Smith, cargo manager for Korean Airlines Ltd.
The North American has maintained the recovery from the lower levels seen during the summer, with good fourth quarter seasonal demand.
However average market rates are steady at 0.63 stg a kg per 100 kg to New York's JFK, 0.73 stg to Los Angeles but firmer to Chicago at 0.74 stg from the previous 0.72 stg.
Some industry sources also said that sterling's growing strength against the U.S. dollar may begin to impact on British exports if it continues.
"The market is very strong. We're seeing very high load factors, with a daily average of 88 to 92 percent of capacity," said American Airlines cargo manager, John Smith.
"But business is not as good as in 1994 at this time of year, but better than last year," he added.
The boom in global telecommunications, including cellular telephones, is helping to fuel demand for airfreight, he said with Latin American a major import market.
Separately other air cargo industry sources said there were backlogs in traffic being handled at Miama, reflecting the latter's key role as Latin America's air cargo hub.

Some agents and airlines are looking at ways to dodge Miami's logjams by shifting cargo through Miami to South America by developing an alternative gateway. This could be based in the Caribbean and utilise planes with spare cargo capacity as their main business is taking tourists from Europe, Canada and the U.S.

Another airline manager said the congestion at Miami is working against European carriers who might normally want to use Miami for ex-Europe cargo but find they are having to take their turn behind U.S. and Canadian originated cargo.

Major European carriers reported good business from the U.K. to South America with south bound planes more heavily booked especially with pharmaceuticals and car parts. North bound traffic includes produce from Venezuela, meat from Argentina and fish from Chile.

Average market rates for a 100 kg to South America excluding the surcharge were unchanged to slightly firmer with Sao Paulo indicated at 2.06 stg a kilo whilst Buenos Aires was likewise little altered at around 2.25 stg a kilo.

Although the main carriers matched the BA surcharges, the smaller ones have not and one agent said that none of the airlines he represents to Central and South America with a weekly lift from Europe of some 80 tonnes have moved to do so. But if any does any surcharge would have to be passed onto to shippers, he added.

Most airlines operating to the Middle East from the U.K. reported a good level of business with most activity eastwards. Middle Eastern based airlines are starting to follow BA's surcharge. Emirates is introducing surcharges at BA's six pence a kilo on Friday November 15 with Gulf Air following at the same rate the next day. Middle East Airlines and the smaller British Mediterranean Airways have not yet introduced surcharges.
Some airline cargo officials said the main objection from forwarders is this lack of uniformity on timing from airlines which makes the forwarders job more complex.

Airlines said the continued absence of the twice weekly Trans Mediterranean Airways (TMA) Boeing 707 service to Beirut has kept upward pressure on rates although TMA hopes to announce on Monday a resumption of this service on Thursday Nove
The European market has also picked up, reflecting some improvement in the economic situation, but also demand from Central and Eastern Europe, industry sources said.

However business is not as strong as might be expected at this time of year, although some sources suggested that a further upturn could be about to start. At Lufthansa,, which expects to see business peaking towards the year-end, Steve Stewart said capacity constraints are having an effect on business. The carrier's Flash express product continues to do well, and is expected to be promoted aggresively in early 1997.
Rates to Stockholm moved to an average 0.73 stg a kg for a 100 kg from 0.72 stg with Copenhagen also firmer at 0.69 stg from the previous 0.65 stg.

New entrants to the South African in recent months means additional capacity is contributing to rates pressure and traffic volumes fluctuate. Average rates are around the 1.80 stg a kg for a 100 kg, little changed on the previous report, although higher on quality direct carriers . -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
